verses.text: When Jesus had finished saying these things, He left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan.
Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them there.
Then some Pharisees came and tested Him by asking, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?"
Jesus answered, "Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator 'made them male and female,'
and said, 'For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh'?
So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate."
"Why then," they asked, "did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away?"
Jesus replied, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning.
Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery."
His disciples said to Him, "If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry."
"Not everyone can accept this word," He replied, "but only those to whom it has been given.

For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it."
Then little children were brought to Jesus for Him to place His hands on them and pray for them. And the disciples rebuked those who brought them.
But Jesus said, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these."
And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there.
Just then a man came up to Jesus and inquired, "Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?"
"Why do you ask Me about what is good?" Jesus replied. "There is only One who is good. If you want to enter life, keep the commandments."
"Which ones?" the man asked. Jesus answered, "'Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness,
honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself.'"
"All these I have kept," said the young man. "What do I still lack?"
Jesus told him, "If you want to be perfect, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me."
When the young man heard this, he went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.
Then Jesus said to His disciples, "Truly I tell you, it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.
Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God."
When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and asked, "Who then can be saved?"
Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible."
"Look," Peter replied, "we have left everything to follow You. What then will there be for us?"

Jesus said to them, "Truly I tell you, in the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne, you who have followed Me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of My name will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative interwoven with teaching — a series of encounters (Pharisees, children, a rich young man, Peter) as Jesus journeys toward Jerusalem.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers navigating real debates of the day — rabbinic schools of thought on divorce, the value of children, and the tension between wealth and discipleship.
context.setting: Jesus has left Galilee for Judea, in the region of Perea under Herod Antipas. The Pharisees' question about divorce (v.3) drops Him into a live rabbinic debate between the schools of Hillel (permitting divorce for almost any reason) and Shammai (permitting it only for sexual immorality) — Jesus sidesteps both schools by returning to Genesis itself.
context.custom: Divorce certificates (get) and marriage contracts (ketubot) from this era are attested in surviving first-century papyri, confirming the legal practice Jesus is questioned about. Patriarchs traditionally blessed children by laying hands on them (as in Genesis 48:14) — the custom the parents in v.13 are seeking from Jesus.
context.timelineImmediate: Marks Jesus' departure from Galilee toward Judea and, ultimately, Jerusalem — the geographic shift mirrors the narrative's shift toward the cross, which the next chapter's third passion prediction makes explicit.
context.timelineBible: Jesus grounds His entire teaching on marriage not in later Mosaic law but in the original creation account (v.4-5, quoting Genesis 1:27 and 2:24) — treating Genesis as the standard even Moses' later concession (v.8) had departed from.

translation.meaning: Quoting Genesis 2:24 directly — describes a union so complete it's treated as a single entity, the basis for Jesus' teaching against divorce.
A stubborn, unyielding resistance — Jesus frames Moses' divorce allowance as a concession to human failure, not God's original design.

occurrences.note: Used only three times in the whole New Testament — twice by Jesus about the Pharisees and once about His own disciples' unbelief after the resurrection.

translation.meaning: Complete or mature, the same word used in the Sermon on the Mount (5:48) — not flawlessness, but wholehearted devotion.
A small sewing-needle opening — the image stresses genuine impossibility by human effort alone, resolved only by God's power (v.26).

gospelParallels.note: Mark's fuller parallel account covering divorce, the children, and the rich young man in sequence.
Luke's shorter version of the children being blessed and the rich ruler's question.

otBackground.note: The creation account Jesus quotes directly as the foundation for His teaching on marriage.
The Mosaic divorce provision the Pharisees cite, which Jesus reframes as a concession rather than the ideal.
The commandments Jesus lists to the rich young man, drawn directly from the Law.

context.sparkNotes: Jesus teaches that marriage is a permanent union and welcomes the children His disciples try to send away. His teaching is grounded directly in Genesis 1:27 and 2:24's "one flesh" language — treating the creation account, not just later Mosaic law, as the real standard.

commentary.note: Henry extends the camel image with real feeling: a rich man, he says, is fittingly compared to a camel because he carries his wealth the way a camel carries its load — it isn't truly his, he received it from others, spends it for others, and must shortly leave it to others. He reads Jesus' closing words to the disciples not as closing the door on the rich young man, but as leaving room for mercy still to reach him.

JFB is precise about where Jesus grounds His teaching on marriage: not in later Mosaic regulation, but in "the original constitution of man as one pair, a male and a female," by God's own design at creation — the divorce debate, in their reading, was never really about interpreting a loophole, but about which starting point defines marriage in the first place.

Gill reads the Pharisees' motive plainly: they came not for the sake of learning, but as spies, watching for any opportunity to expose Jesus to public hatred. On Moses' divorce provision, he draws a careful distinction — it was God permitting an accommodation through Moses' civil law, not God's own original design, which is exactly the difference Jesus presses in His answer.
